from IPython.display import Markdown, display
import requests

# Going to get the data
url = "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/"
path = "adamrossnelson/why-program/refs/heads/main/"
file = "Py-script-Qmd-notebook-comparisons.txt"

response = requests.get(url + path + file, timeout=15)
response.raise_for_status()
my_text = response.text
display(Markdown(my_text))

Comparing .py Files and .qmd Files for Working with Python
When you start learning Python, one of the first things you have to decide is where you are going to actually write your code. Two common options are a plain Python script, which is a file that ends in .py, and a Quarto document, which is a file that ends in .qmd. Both files let you write and run Python code, but they are built for different purposes, and the difference matters a lot for people who want to do data science.
A .py file is a plain text file that contains only Python code. When you open one, you see instructions for the computer from top to bottom, and that is basically all you see. To run the code, you hand the whole file to Python and it executes every line in order, start to finish. In a .py file, you cannot easily include nicely formatted explanations, headings, bulleted lists, tables, images, charts or other contextual information. A .py file is best when you want to build a program or a tool that runs from beginning to end. However, a .py file is less friendly when your real goal is to think, explore, explain, and share.
A .qmd file is a Quarto document. It is also a plain text file, but it is designed to mix three things together in one place. In this one place you have written explanations in normal English (or other human-spoken languages), blocks of Python code, and the results of that Python code. You write your prose the way you would write a short article or a lab notebook. When you render the document, Quarto runs the code, captures the output, and produces a polished final product such as a web page, a PDF, or a slide deck. The code, the words, and the results all live together and stay in sync.
For someone who is brand new to Python and brand new to programming, the .qmd style is often much more helpful to learn first. First, a .qmd lets you think out loud. You can write a sentence describing what you are about to try, then try it, then write another sentence about what happened. That habit is exactly how learning works, and a plain .py script does not encourage this explain-do-reflect (try-look-adjust) cycle. Second, it lets you run code in small pieces instead of all at once. You can execute a single block, look at the result, adjust, and run it again. That tight loop of try-look-adjust is how data scientists actually work, and it is how beginners build confidence without feeling overwhelmed. Third, it keeps your explanations and your results permanently attached to each other. Six months from now, when you or someone else opens the file, the chart is right next to the sentence that says what the chart is supposed to show. Fourth, it produces something you can share. A rendered Quarto document looks like a real report, so you can hand it to a teacher, a teammate, or a manager without any extra cleanup. Fifth, it supports headings, lists, images, links, and mathematical notation, so your document can grow up with you as your projects become more serious. For a data scientist, whose job is not only to compute answers but also to communicate them clearly, this combination of live code and readable narrative is a very large advantage.
A short note on Jupyter notebooks. You may hear about Jupyter notebooks, which use files that end in .ipynb. They are another popular way to mix code, results, and explanation, and they share many of the benefits of .qmd files described above. Quarto documents and Jupyter notebooks are cousins in that sense, and if you meet Jupyter first, you are not doing anything wrong. Quarto builds on the same idea and adds some additional strengths around producing polished, shareable final documents. Jupyter notebooks deserve a friendly acknowledgment, and most data scientists will eventually need to be fully capable of working with both Jupyter notebooks and Quarto notebooks. Choosing Quarto as a place to start learning is a sensible choice.
In short, reach for a .py file when you are writing a program that just needs to run. Reach for a .qmd file when you are learning, exploring data, or telling the story of what you found, which is most of the time in data science.


From here we can begin “analyzing” this text.

display(Markdown(f"There are {len(my_text)} characters in this text"))

There are 4155 characters in this text


Lets ask how many capital letters are there in this text.

print("T".isupper())
print("t".isupper())

True
False



num_upper = 0

for l in my_text:
    if l.isupper(): num_upper += 1

display(
    Markdown(
        f"There are {num_upper} capital upper case characters in this text."))

There are 65 capital upper case characters in this text.
